title: Is Technology Making High School a Joke? September 27, 2026
author: Gary Houchens
source: Gary Houchens (garyhouchens.substack.com), column for the Bowling Green Daily News,
summary: Houchens, writing in his Bowling Green Daily News column, challenges high school educators to ask students about their screen time and take the answers seriously. He draws on the Fordham Institute study 'High Tech, Low Standards', which found most students spend over half of class time on school-issued devices and that large shares use phones or school computers for social media, video and shopping. The survey also found substantial AI use for solving math problems, summarizing reading and drafting essays, and a belief among many students that homework has become meaningless. His reading is that technology has made high school a bit of a joke and that the vast amount of technology placed in front of students accelerates avoidance of real work. He recommends rolling back screen time, returning to textbooks and paper, enforcing meaningful phone bans, and teaching a rich curriculum so students can evaluate AI output.
points: School-issued one-to-one devices mean most students spend the majority of class time on screens, before counting prohibited phone use.
Heavy technology users in the Fordham study were also more likely to say missing school would not hurt their grades, linking tech use to absenteeism.
Students report using AI to solve math, avoid reading and draft essays, and many say it has made homework meaningless.
Proposed responses include less in-class screen time, paper-based performance tasks, and real enforcement of phone bans.
A knowledge-rich curriculum is needed so students have the background to judge AI output, with AI used to extend learning, not replace it.
quotes: A new research study by the Fordham Institute surveyed 2,000 current high school students or recent high school graduates about their use of technology during the school day.
62% of students report they spend more than half their class time every day on a school-issued device. One third of students said they spend more than 75% of their school day on screens.
Forty-eight percent of students said they had used artificial intelligence to solve math problems for them, while 36% avoid reading requirement books or texts by having AI summarize for them.

My takeaway is that for far too many students, technology has made high school a bit of a joke. Not only are students using it to avoid meaningful work, but they are also spending valuable instruction time playing games, doomscrolling, and even gambling online.
But what is new is the vast amount of technology we’ve deliberately stuck in front of them to enable and accelerate the problem.

Put away the laptops for a while and give students textbooks and paper notebooks once again. Ask them to complete performance tasks demonstrating their knowledge and skill without the benefit of a computer.
Educators should insist on exposing students to a rich, complex curriculum that gives them the background knowledge to critically evaluate AI outputs.
Above all, educators must invite students to use AI to enhance and extend their learning rather than replace it.
